analysis.title: The week in seven charts: Wall Street's biggest one-day loss of value on record
key_insights: The S&P 500 fell 4.4% to 7,354 on Thursday 5 November. The Nasdaq 100 fell about 6.4% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) fell 12.3%, leaving chipmakers close to 38% below their June high.
Breadth was extremely weak: decliners outnumbered advancers by more than five to one, and 84% of the day's turnover was in falling names.
About $2.8tn of US market value was lost in one day, the largest on record, above the earlier high of about $2.69tn during the pandemic sell-off.

Syz attributes the selloff to politics. Wednesday's post-election bounce (relief the vote was over, hopes of a split Congress) faded within 24 hours. Investors turned to what a stronger Democratic showing, especially in state capitals, means for the AI build-out: power and water demand, planning approvals and rising data centre construction costs. A weak Qualcomm earnings outlook added pressure on chips.

The Nasdaq Composite's 5.52% drop is its eighth fall of more than 5% since 2015. Of the seven earlier cases, 6 bounced the next session, 5 were lower seven days later, and 6 were higher three months later, with an average gain of 23%. Three of the seven cases are from March 2020, so the sample is thin.

Since 30 June, 12-month forward EPS estimates rose 32% for memory makers, 31% for AI infrastructure and 30% for semiconductors overall. Forward P/E ratios fell 50%, 36% and 35% for those groups. All 20 S&P 500 chip companies trade on a lower multiple.

J.P. Morgan Market Intelligence says S&P 500 returns after US midterm elections since 1990 average 5.4% at three months, 11.4% at six, 12.5% at nine and 14.7% at twelve months. The index has never been lower at the six, nine and twelve-month marks.

J.P. Morgan says the latest risk reduction is short of full capitulation. Systematic selling and crowded technology positions remain threats. Heavy deleveraging and momentum exposure at only 30% of its high suggest conditions could support an alpha recovery.
Syz argues the S&P 500 and US federal debt have risen under presidents of both parties, and that continued public borrowing and solid nominal growth should support equities.

Syz sees no reason for the AI and data centre investment cycle to wind down in the near term. It cites the Biden-era CHIPS Act and export restrictions on chip-making tools, and says AI and data centres are now treated as national security and economic strength issues.

market_movers.rationale: A weak earnings outlook from Qualcomm weighed on the chip sector on 5 November.

sector_views.rationale: The SOX fell 12.3% in one day and is about 38% below its June high. Forward EPS estimates rose about 30% since 30 June while forward P/E fell about 35%. Syz does not give a rating.
Syz sees no reason for the AI and data centre investment cycle to wind down in the near term, citing national security framing and bipartisan policy support.

earnings_insights: Qualcomm gave a weak earnings outlook that weighed on chip stocks (reported around 5 November, no figures given).
Since 30 June, 12-month forward EPS estimates rose 32% for memory makers, 31% for AI infrastructure and 30% for semiconductors overall (analyst estimates, not reported results).
risk_factors: Systematic selling and crowded technology positions could extend the selloff.
A stronger Democratic showing could slow the AI build-out through power and water constraints, planning approvals and higher data centre costs.
A first bounce after a 5% Nasdaq drop does not guarantee the selloff is over: 5 of 7 prior cases were lower seven days later.

tension_points.bull_case: Syz sees AI and data centre spending as a national security priority backed by the CHIPS Act and export controls, so the investment cycle should continue. Forward EPS estimates for chips are up about 30% since 30 June.
tension_points.bear_case: Investors worry a stronger Democratic showing could constrain the build-out through power and water demand, planning approvals and rising data centre construction costs. Chip valuations fell 35% to 50% and systematic selling plus crowded tech positions remain threats.
